record.original_question: Is it consistent that the continuum c is strictly larger than ℵ2 and that for every cardinal κ in the interval [ℵ1, c], every 2-coloring of κ×ω has a monochromatic rectangle of sizes κ and ω, i.e. \( inom{\kappa}{\omega} 	o  inom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2\)?

evidence.quote: Problem 2.13. Is it consistent that c > ℵ2 and (κ over ω) → (κ over ω)^(1,1)_2 for every κ ∈ [ℵ1, c]?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For an infinite cardinal κ, write
\[
\binom{\kappa}{\omega}\to\binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_{2}
\]
to mean that for every 2-coloring c : κ × ω → {0,1} there exist sets A ⊆ κ and B ⊆ ω with |A| = κ and |B| = ω such that c is constant on A × B.

Let c = 2^{ℵ_0} denote the cardinality of the continuum.

Question: Is it consistent with ZFC that c > ℵ_2 and that for every cardinal κ with ℵ_1 ≤ κ ≤ c one has
\[
\binom{\kappa}{\omega}\to\binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_{2}\,?
\]
artifact.status_search_result: Known consistency results of Garti and Shelah establish that the strong polarized relation can hold simultaneously for all cardinals in [ℵ_1, c] when c = ℵ_2, and that the relation is consistent at the continuum more generally. However, web searches did not surface a published result settling the consistency of the conjunction "c > ℵ_2" with the simultaneous relation across the entire interval [ℵ_1, c]. The status appears to remain unresolved in the available literature.

status_evidence.title: Strong Polarized Relations for the Continuum
status_evidence.snippet: The strong polarized relation θ → θ^{1,1}_2 applied simultaneously for every θ in [ℵ_1, 2^{ℵ_0}] is consistent with ZFC.
status_evidence.claim: Consistency of the simultaneous relation across [ℵ_1, c] is established, but typical models have c = ℵ_2.

status_evidence.title: Partition Calculus and Cardinal Invariants (arXiv:1112.5772)
status_evidence.snippet: Polarized partition relations and their interaction with cardinal characteristics of the continuum.
status_evidence.claim: Related results, but no resolution of the c > ℵ_2 case for the full interval.
